The prompt notes that Popper himself preferred better-corroborated theories when choosing which theory to *act on*. If this preference were merely a non-rational psychological leap indistinguishable in practice from acting on higher probability, it would functionally reintroduce the inductive principle Popper rejected: that past success (corroboration) is a reliable guide for future action. By labeling it 'non-rational,' the target avoids explaining why Popper specifically chose the *better-corroborated* theory rather than any other theory for action. If the choice is guided by corroboration status, it implies a rational link between past test survival and future reliability, which smuggles induction back in under the guise of 'psychological necessity.'
